modules.name: Orientation: The Map and the Lantern

lessons.title: The hidden curriculum
lessons.idea: CS teaches theory, IS teaches business systems; the day-to-day tooling is learned by apprenticeship, forums and breaking things
lessons.summary: Building with AI runs on everyday tools that school rarely teaches, so the gap is in the syllabus, not in you. This lesson shows why, and lays out the map every later lesson is shelved on.

lessons.title: The map of everything
lessons.idea: One picture: your computer → the network → the internet → services → AI, and where every later lesson sits
lessons.summary: Everything you build with AI sits on one road with five stops (your computer, the network, the internet, services, AI), so when something breaks, ask which stop first. This lesson draws that road and gives every later lesson its place on it.

lessons.title: How old is all this?
lessons.idea: A timeline from Unix (1969) to MCP (2024) — most of it is older than you think, the AI layer is brand new
lessons.summary: The ideas under your tools are decades old, but old does not mean frozen: versions change every year, security changes fastest (text codes to authenticator apps to passkeys, broken hashes, retired TLS) and AI on top changes fastest of all, so learn the ideas once, check the version, and assume old login advice is out of date.

lessons.title: Model vs app vs agent
lessons.idea: GPT/Claude/Gemini (models) vs the apps wrapping them vs agents that act
lessons.summary: The model is the engine (a lab's file of numbers: text in, text out, no memory), the app is the car built around it (chat window, saved chats, hidden instructions, the bill), and an agent is that car allowed to drive, with tools, a loop and you deciding what it may do.

lessons.title: How AI models work today
lessons.idea: ~20 min. Five years of change: LLMs → multimodal models (see/hear/generate, some via API), diffusion models (image, video, audio; rarely text); tokens, context and why models degrade as it fills; memory and RAG (chat search, self-kept memory, files/Notion via tools); system prompts and injected instruction files (CLAUDE.md); settings (temperature, top-p...); caching and token billing (input, output, cache write, cache read); modes (chat, Cowork, Code) and platforms (web, desktop, CLI, cloud); skills vs connectors vs plugins and their marketplaces; individual vs enterprise; other surfaces (Claude Design, voice modes); personal agents (OpenClaw and similar). Brief here, own lessons later
lessons.summary: Underneath it all is still a model that only knows what is on its desk right now; nearly everything new in the last five years (multimodal hand-offs, diffusion, memory and RAG, instruction files, caching, modes, plugins, plans and always-on agents) is about what gets put on that desk, what it hands off to other models, and where the desk sits.

lessons.title: Trust what you can verify
lessons.idea: Agents now write, run and debug their own code, so hand-coding and hand-debugging are nearly obsolete; your new job is judging what you cannot see: security holes in code that works, team norms and the project's chosen libraries (AI drifts and keeps adding dependencies), and "ready to deploy" claims. You can only trust AI on what it can verify; past that, learn to check it yourself or bring in an expert
lessons.summary: You can only trust AI on what can actually be checked: agents now fix their own crashes, so your job is judging what they cannot see (security holes in code that works, team norms, dependencies, "ready to deploy"), and past that line you either learn to check it or bring in someone who can.

lessons.title: Files are just bytes
lessons.idea: A .py file is a text file; the extension is a label that tells the OS which program opens it
lessons.summary: Every file is just a row of numbers called bytes, and the extension is a label on its name that picks which program opens it, not what is inside; this lesson draws that picture so nothing an agent does with your files surprises you.

lessons.title: File extensions & associations
lessons.idea: Showing hidden extensions, renaming .txt → .py, "Open with", default apps
lessons.summary: The extension is a label in a file's name and your computer keeps a ledger matching each label to a program, so renaming changes the label but never the bytes, while Open with set to Always and default apps edit the ledger; this lesson draws that picture as of October 2026, with AI tools now making the files.

lessons.title: Folders, paths & the working directory
lessons.idea: Absolute vs relative paths, C:\ vs /, why "run it from the right folder" matters
lessons.summary: A path is an address, and a relative path only makes sense from the working directory of the program that reads it.

lessons.title: Hidden files & dotfiles
lessons.idea: .git, .env, .venv, AppData, ~/.config — the invisible config layer
lessons.summary: Almost every project and app keeps its settings, history, secrets and now its AI instructions in files your computer hides or tucks out of the way, and hidden only means out of sight, never locked.

lessons.title: Environment variables & PATH
lessons.idea: How typing python finds the right program; why "not recognized as a command" happens
lessons.summary: Every program starts with a copy of its parent's settings, its environment, and PATH in it is an ordered list of folders where the first match wins, so which program runs and which keys it can see depend on who started it and when.

latest.title: Environment variables & PATH
latest.idea: How typing python finds the right program; why "not recognized as a command" happens
latest.summary: Every program starts with a copy of its parent's settings, its environment, and PATH in it is an ordered list of folders where the first match wins, so which program runs and which keys it can see depend on who started it and when.

first.title: The hidden curriculum
first.idea: CS teaches theory, IS teaches business systems; the day-to-day tooling is learned by apprenticeship, forums and breaking things
first.summary: Building with AI runs on everyday tools that school rarely teaches, so the gap is in the syllabus, not in you. This lesson shows why, and lays out the map every later lesson is shelved on.
